title: Four dangers for a swimmer
hookLine: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks: the dangers for someone new to the path

cards: About five hundred monks arrive at a village called Cātumā with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, some of them newly ordained, and they're loud: greeting the resident monks, finding beds, arranging bowls and robes, all at once.

The Buddha hears the noise and sends them all away. The local people and, the sutta says, a god named Brahmā Sahampati plead for them: they're new, like young seedlings that need water. The Buddha relents.
And then, with the new ones sitting in front of him, he tells them what tends to drown beginners.

teach.b: Someone wading into a river, the sutta says, can expect four dangers: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks. The Buddha names each one for a person who has just entered the training.
The waves are anger at being taught. Do this, don't do that, look ahead, look behind, wear your robe this way.
Someone used to giving instructions at home now takes them from people younger than they are, and it stings; a person like this, the sutta says, can give up the training right there.
The crocodiles are the stomach: eat this, don't eat that, not now.
The whirlpools are the five kinds of sensual pleasure, what's lovely to see, hear, smell, taste and touch, swirling around a new monk when he walks into the village.

The sharks are sexual desire. The text, spoken to monks, names it through women; read today, it's the pull of attraction for anyone in training who has vowed celibacy. None of the four is deep philosophy.
What sends a beginner home is being corrected, food, the things to want, attraction.

Knowing the water doesn't make the crocodile go away. But a beginner who's been told the waves will come can feel one and think, ah, this is the wave they meant, instead of, this proves I don't belong here.

how: Some monastic teachers use this sutta with new monks and nuns, so that the frustration of being corrected or the pull of food and pleasure can be recognized as a stage of training, not a reason to leave.

o: a river spirit said to guard new monks from harm
the Pali name for a crocodile in the river
the village where new monks heard of four dangers

games.q: the four dangers: tap the pairs.
p: the five kinds of sensual pleasure

s: the Buddha first sent the noisy new monks away
the people of Cātumā and Brahmā Sahampati pleaded for them, and he relented.
the waves stand for deep philosophical doubts
they're anger and frustration at being instructed.
the dangers come from the village, not from inside the beginner
all four are inner pulls: resentment, appetite, pleasure, desire.

games.q: you're new to a practice, and someone younger corrects how you sit. you feel a flash of anger. in this sutta's picture, what is it?
games.why: the waves are anger at being taught. the sutta names them so a beginner can recognize them, not drown in them.

practice: Think of something you've started recently and want to keep, a practice, a job, a way of living, and ask gently: what are my waves, my crocodile, my whirlpool, my shark? Give each a short, silent name.
Then let the names go and rest with the breath, like floating.

wordCard.voice: Catuma. Waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks: anger at being taught, the stomach, the five pleasures, and desire.

carryVoice: Your line: know the water. A wave you can name is easier to swim through. That's plenty for today.
